utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One preliminary matter and it's this: The Trial Chamber today heard an application in closed session in relation to the evidence of a particular witness. The application was for the evidence to be heard in closed session. The Trial Chamber rejected the application, the nature of the evidence not being such that, when weighed against the need for a public trial, that such an order was warranted. The transcript of the ruling will be released in due course. Yes. We'll hear the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Andras Riedlmayer. Your Honours, the Chamber as well as the amici and the accused, they have the report that is entitled "The Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Kosovo 1998, 1999." The report's composed by an executive summary and although the survey contains a database of approximately hundreds of sites, the Prosecution has just disclosed extracts related to the sites alleged in the indictment. In arriving at The Hague, Mr. Riedlmayer, he brought with him blown-up photos and photos with a better quality of the indictment sites as well as some additional photos. They are the same photos that we have already disclosed but they are in a better quality. And the Prosecution produced this booklet containing the summary report and all the photos separated in order by the indictment sites, and so we propose to introduce this as an exhibit. And that will be used by Mr. Riedlmayer during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Romano, you can take this evidence fairly shortly since we have the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. I just would like to make it easy for the Court to be able to understand and later on to use the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I give you the copies? And, Your Honours, I also don't think the Chamber has Mr. Riedlmayer's curriculum vitae, what I would propose to introduce as an exhibit, and instead of going through it in detail and just ask a few questions about his experience and education.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 88.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have here the curriculum and copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you please state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Andras Janos Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You're currently the bibliographer for the Documentation Center for Islamic Architecture, Aga Khan Program, Fine Arts Library at Harvard University?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And according to your CV, you have university degree, more specifically, two masters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between answer and question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- and in library --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And from Princeton, and in Library and Information Science from Simmons College of Boston?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: For several years, you have been focused on the study of documentation of destruction of cultural heritage. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And as an art documentation specialist, when and how did you get involved in the research and study of destruction of cultural heritage, and particularly in the Balkans region?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I've been working as an art documentation specialist for more than 15 years. I've been working on the study of the history and culture of the Balkans for some 30 years now. In the late 1980s, I was working on a project on the protection of cultural property in armed conflict and compiling a bibliography on it. When the conflict in the Balkans broke out, I immediately saw reports of the destruction of cultural property and I started collecting information with a view towards studying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you just briefly describe any prior works that you have done in this field --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- before the Kosovo project.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: During the war in Bosnia between 1992 and 1995, I did a series of studies on the destruction of libraries and archives and the destruction of historical architecture. Some of these were published, others were presented as documentary films. And I also testified before the Commission for Security and Cooperation in Europe on cultural destruction in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And the articles and the lectures are all listed in your curriculum --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's correct? Mr. Riedlmayer, I would like to just go into the background of the survey, the background of the report. As you said, in the course of your work in 1998, you became aware of the fact that in Kosova, various sites of cultural heritage were possibly being damaged or destroyed. From that time, you started to collect the information. Can you just tell the Court what kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: When the conflict began in 1998, there were reports in the media, starting in the summer of 1998, that suggested that cultural heritage may have been targeted by either side. There were also various allegations coming from various governmental and unofficial sources. At the time, I was simply at the level of collecting this information. When the war broke out in March with the NATO bombardment of Yugoslavia, the allegations multiplied while the sources of information narrowed considerably because of the absence of independent observers in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the sources that you are referring to, they are listed in Appendix 3 of your report, in pages 23 to 24; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: They are the reports by Yugoslav governmental and professional institutions, and reports by Kosovar refugees, and media accounts; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When and how the idea of a Kosovo cultural heritage project came about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: At the end of hostilities in June of 1999, it was clear to me that someone would have to establish what had happened with regard to cultural heritage in Kosovo. Reporters were flooding back into Kosovo, and while they rarely covered cultural heritage as such, they mentioned the destruction and there were lots of pictures broadcast. I made inquiries with UNESCO to see whether they were pursuing any systematic study, and the answer was no. I put out an Internet appeal, and Mr. Andrew Herscher, an architect whom I had known professionally, approached me with the idea that we should do a study together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So this was when? June?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This was the end of June/beginning of July 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And so you and Mr. Andrew Herscher undertook the project?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And can you just give also to the Court the qualifications of Mr. Herscher?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Herscher is a trained architect. He has degrees in architecture from Princeton University and Harvard University and is completing a doctorate in architectural history, theory, and criticism. He has also worked in the Balkans for the past ten years, including assessment of war damage in Mostar after the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how did you and Mr. Herscher, how did you obtain funding for the project?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We first approached Harvard's Centre for Middle Eastern Studies to ask if they would act as our institutional sponsors for such a project. After they indicated that they would be agreeable, we approached the Packard Humanities Institute, an American-registered charity that supports conservation of archeological sites and cultural heritage, and they agreed to provide funding for the expenses of our project.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the goals of the Kosovo project?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Our project had three basic goals. One was to establish the fact of what had happened, the second was to provide a basis for post-war reconstruction, and the third was to provide material that could be useful to the ICTY in its work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, could you kindly put a pause between the question and answer. Bear in mind the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Riedlmayer, can you just wait after I make my question until you answer, otherwise it won't be possible for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, the study focused on damage to architectural heritage from the three major religious communities: Islamic, Roman Catholic and Serb Orthodox, as well as damage to the historical civil architecture; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how did you and Mr. Herscher -- sorry. No. First, can you give us a brief overview what constitutes an Islamic, Roman Catholic, or Serbian Orthodox site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Those are the three principal religious communities in Kosovo. Each of them has houses of worship. In addition to houses of worship, there are also other buildings. In the case of Islamic, the house of worship would be a mosque or a dervish lodge or a tekke or Koran schools and other educational institutions, also religious libraries and archives. In the case of the two Christian communities, the Catholic and the Serbian Orthodox, we are dealing primarily with churches and monasteries, but the Serbian Orthodox Church also has a seminary in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Among all the sites that are listed in Kosovo, how did you and Mr. Herscher select the ones to be included in the survey?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We based our work on several categories. First we surveyed the published literature on heritage in Kosovo, the publications of the Monuments Protection authorities, and the scientific literature. From that we compiled a list, as well as any published pre-war documentation on these sites. Our second category was sites about which there had been allegations of damage. These are the allegations listed in Appendix number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Approximately how many sites in total the survey contain?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The survey has 560 sites, which actually covers a larger number of buildings because some sites have more than one building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And that includes religious sites and also civil architecture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: After the sites were selected, the database was developed, the information was gathered, you start the research, and you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We did our first fieldwork in Kosovo during the month of October 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Was it at that time that you also had contact with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped at The Hague on our way to Kosovo, and we had a meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the nature of the meeting and the conversations that you had with representatives of the office?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We first asked them -- asked the Office of the Prosecutor whether they would be interested in the kind of information that we were collecting. They answered in the affirmative. They also told us that we would not be acting as agents of the Tribunal. They also indicated some of the kinds of things that would be useful for their work, things that we might not have thought of on our own. For example, the importance of obtaining recent pre-destruction photos, if possible, of damaged sites. They also indicated that in the event we should encounter eyewitnesses to the destruction, we were to take basic information and names and contact but that we were not to conduct extended witness interviews, that the Tribunal would take care of that. Our main task was to document the damage to the architecture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. In total, how long it took to develop your project and how many times, how many trips did you make to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The project took approximately two years to complete, in the course of which we made three trips to Kosovo of roughly three weeks each. Our first trip was in October of 1999, and there were follow-up trips in October of 2000 and March of 2001. The survey was finished in the summer of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'm going to ask you to briefly describe first the methodology used and the sources used in your report, and second, I will ask you to explain the categories used to assess the damage and destruction recorded. So first, the methodology and the sources.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I indicated, our first step was to do research, before heading into the field, to see what documentation existed of the pre-war condition of these buildings. We took this along to Kosovo, and as we visited each site, there would be a series of steps that we would then take. The first step would be to go to a location and identify and verify the site. This was done by interviewing locals but also by comparing our pre-war documentation. In the case of a building that was totally destroyed, if we had plans, you could trace the foundations. If one had pre-war photographs, surrounding buildings would still offer identification of the site. Once we had done this, we would then take several photographs to document the site, and Mr. Herscher and I would consult with each other and agree on the description and categorical assessment of the damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, before we go to the categories, I think that in Appendix 2 of your report, pages 17 to 22, apart from the field assessment made by you and Mr. Herscher that you have just described, there is also a description, that of other sources, of various other sources that you used for the sites that you have not visited. So can you just explain that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: If you -- if you need to use the report, with the assistance of the usher, maybe we can put the report on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness -- let the witness have his report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, then, if that's the idea. Have we got a spare copy so that the witness can have one? One for the ELMO. That's right. And then the witness can have his.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So in order of presentation, the first one was our field investigations which I have described.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And how many -- how many sites did you and Mr. Herscher visit in person?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We visited approximately 144 sites in person. The second largest group of sites are those documented by the International Management Group, an intergovernmental organisation which was commissioned by the European Union to conduct an assessment of damage to buildings and infrastructure in Kosovo. Their work was completed in the spring of 2000, and we were able to obtain a copy of their database during our second visit to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you can go very briefly on the sources. Just mention the name and a brief, a short, short explanation.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The other two -- the other three main sources were the three religious communities; the Serbian Orthodox Patriarchate, with which we exchanged documentation - they also have published a great deal of their documentation - the Roman Catholic Diocese, we had interviews with clergy; and the Islamic community, which had a very large archive of photographs collected by Professor Sabri Bajgora, who is the assistant mufti of Kosovo. We also had information from the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Kosovo, the local institute in Djakovica, UNMIK's Department of Urban Planning in Pec, and a number of private individuals who are named in that appendix. Finally, we also took account of media accounts. We never included any sites on the sole authority of media accounts, but where first-hand media reports were available, we included them and identified them as such. As Your Honours will note, in many cases these sources were cross-corroborated with each other, and in all cases, we included only sites for which photographic documentation was available.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. So we passed through the methodology and the sources. Can you right now please walk us through the categories of assessment of damages --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- established.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Initially we had in mind using UNHCR's categories. However, we found that they were designed for housing and not necessarily appropriate for historical monuments, especially since we were doing the survey in part with establishing the feasibility of reconstruction in mind. Category 1 is self-explanatory. It's "undamaged buildings." "Lightly damaged" is a rather large category, and we were extremely conservative in assigning it in the sense that it covers any damage that does not impair the main structure of the building. This means that it includes everything from vandalism and small fires set in the building to shell holes in the wall to even a minaret or a steeple blown up but the main structure remaining intact. Part of the roof could be smashed, but if the roof as a whole was still okay and the perimeter walls were standing, we called it lightly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: "Heavily damaged" is any structure that has suffered significant structural damage to its main elements. Typically, it would be a building that was completely burnt out, often with roof collapsed, major blast damage, damage to perimeter walls. "Almost destroyed" is the next-to-last category. This would be a building which was missing some of its principal parts, like one or more of the perimeter walls, which would require complete reconstruction but which still had some elements standing. "Completely destroyed" is again self-explanatory. It's a building which had no reusable parts left standing above ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. So as a result of your research, you and Mr. Herscher prepared this joint report entitled "The Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Kosovo." And as I explained to the Court before, the report is comprised by a summary of the findings and a database containing all the sites, and with specific and detailed information. It also contains the maps. I would ask you, Mr. Riedlmayer, by using the report that is on the ELMO, if you can briefly walk us through the findings for the destruction of the religious cultural sites: Islamic, Roman Catholic, and Serbian Orthodox. It's pages 7 and 10 of the report.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Just a second. Okay. I've already outlined what constitutes the religious heritage, so I will skip that part. In the case of Islamic architectural heritage, the primary category of buildings that suffered damage was mosques. We are fortunate that we have a published figure for the number of mosques in Kosovo on the eve of the war, and as of 1993, according to the Islamic community, there were 607 mosques in Kosovo. Our documentation showed that more than one-third of these were either destroyed or damaged, and the evidence suggests that this happened in 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the evidence that you had that it happened in 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: There are three kinds of factors that would indicate this. One is the nature of the damage. If the damage is fire, you can often tell if it's recent from things like smell. If the building is burnt out, by the growth of vegetation or otherwise inside. Blast damage certainly indicates that this occurred during some kind of conflict. And vandalism indicates that it was not an accidental event. The second kind of indication is the statements of eyewitnesses, which usually corroborated the evidence of the material evidence. Thirdly, the existence of recent pre-war photographs of the buildings in their undamaged condition suggests that the destruction was in the last few years. Many of our pre-destruction photos come from 1997, so it makes very clear that the destruction happened subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In your report, you give us an approximate figure how many mosques were damaged in 1998, 1999. Can you give us this figure?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly 225.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The next one would be the Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. There was much less information available concerning Roman Catholic sites, mainly because, first of all, there were fewer of them - the Roman Catholic community is the smallest of the three communities in Kosovo - but also because there appeared to be a great deal less damage to Catholic sites. In many places where housing and Islamic monuments had been destroyed in large proportion, Catholic monuments remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And the Serbian Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Kosovo is known as the site of many of the most important monuments of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and these are probably the best-published monuments of any of the communities in Kosovo, both in terms of pre-war documentation and also in terms of documentation of damage to the monuments. What we tried to do is visit as many of these as possible, concentrating our efforts on monuments that were not well documented already by sources such as the Serbian Orthodox Church. Subsequent to our first visit, we engaged in an exchange of photos and other information with the eparchy of Raske and Prizren. Our findings were, first of all, that the Serbian Orthodox monuments that were alleged to have been destroyed or damaged by NATO, we found no sign of damage that could be attributed to air attacks. We did, however, find that a great many of these monuments, as many as 80 or more, had been damaged after the war, presumably in attacks by returning Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, in your research you also came across several sites claimed by Yugoslav authorities to have either been destroyed or serious damage by the NATO airstrikes, and among them some of the Orthodox churches. In arriving at The Hague, you brought us a photo that I have here with me of the Orthodox church in Dreznic [phoen] -- Dreznic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Drsnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Drsnik. That was claimed to be bombed by NATO, and I have copies of the photos. Can you give us an explanation of what that constitutes? There are two photos. I just have one colour copy, and the others are, unfortunately, black and white for the moment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The curriculum vitae will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 89, and the first picture, Prosecution Exhibit 90.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We made a point of taking all allegations seriously, and that is why we visited almost all of the sites for which damage was claimed by various Yugoslav official bodies during the war. This is a church, the church of St. Paraskeva, in the village of Drsnik, municipality of Klina. According to the Institute for Protection of Monuments of the Republic of Serbia and the Ministry of Information, during the war, according to them, in April of 1999, this church suffered serious damage from NATO bombs. We went to the village and found the church with its roof intact, its modern metal belfry intact. However, clearly a fire had been set inside the building. You can see the smudge marks above the door and the initials "UCK," KLA, scrawled into the soot. Could I have the next picture, please. In the interior of the church, a fire had been set, causing damage to mural paintings on the walls, and in addition, someone had gone there and defaced the murals, again with the initials "UCK," with Xs across the faces of the saints and kings. So we included this in our database, but it's very clear that the damage was not done by bombs but by human beings, from the ground up. According to the Serbian Orthodox Church and news reports, the Serb inhabitants of the village left in the second half of June, so it stands to reason that the damage occurred subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That Serbian Orthodox Church is mentioned -- is the one mentioned in your report on page 9; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 9.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last photograph will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 91.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, also to illustrate the damage to religious sites, after arriving here in The Hague, you produced this chart with one of our investigators, and that will be helpful to illustrate the damage of all three religious sites. If you can give us a brief explanation of the chart.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 92.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a breakdown by the number of buildings in each category. The red columns represent Roman Catholic sites; the yellow columns, Serbian Orthodox sites; and the blue columns, Islamic sites. As you can see, the largest number of damaged sites is definitely Islamic. The "undamaged" columns do not represent by any means the total corpus; we included undamaged buildings only if there had been allegations or if we happened to cross them. But the "damaged" categories are fairly representative of the facts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. As I mentioned before, in your database it contains hundreds of sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: But we have just used the ones that are alleged -- that were mentioned and listed in the indictment. They are organised in the order of the indictment. Can you please walk us through at least two of the sites, the one that you have visited in person and the one that you rely on some other information, and show the Court where can we find the information: the category of the damage, who did it, and the information. So if we can get the report and maybe go for the first site, that is, Celine. It's not numbered, but maybe --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It's right after the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- the number can be helpful. It's K0209346.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: All right. What you see there -- if you could try to get the whole page in. Okay. What you see is a sample page from our database. It's a very simple entry and very typical of the large number of entries where we had very basic kind of information. First all, notice at the bottom the surveyors. In this case, the information comes from -- is corroborated by two third-party sources, the IMG database and Professor Sabri Bajgora of the Islamic community. The second thing, a photograph. We included, as you were told, no information unless we had corroborating photographs. This is an example of a completely destroyed building. As you see, there is very little left of the original structure. The type of information we recorded were the names, if known, the village, the date of construction, the period, whether it had officially protected status, type, setting, building condition and the state of adjacent buildings. You can see adjacent buildings with old roof tiles, so it makes it more likely this structure was singled out rather than hit along with other types.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Maybe you can use the blown-up photo.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. If you go to the next page there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The second -- the next page.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here the -- this, which is either a fragment of an arch or maybe the minaret's broken, it's hard to tell. But you can tell this building next to it has old roof tiles, clearly not a recent repair. So this was an example of the kind of site where we were working with second hand information. For examples of sites that we visited first hand, I would suggest that you go to K029370.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's the Djakovica market. This was under official legal protection. You can see that it had a number of different names it was known by. You can see that the damage report is quite detailed, and we have photos from a variety of sources. One example here of a number of photos we have of the bazaar taken right before the war, one taken during the destruction, by a resident of Gjakove, and on the next page two further photos, one pre-war photo and one after. This is also an example of an informant's statement. Again we merely summarised what we heard, and when we had the opportunity, we obtained contact information. The next page. The next page lists some of our background research under "Bibliography" under pre-war photos as well as media accounts. I'm now turning to two photos past. Yes, this one. This is a photo that we took after the war. You can see the burnt-out shops of the bazaar with the walls in between the burnt-out shops still standing. In the background is the Hadum Mosque. You can see the top of the minaret's been shot off, and there's a hole in the minaret halfway down, from impact of some kind of projectile. The next page. The next page is our entry for the Hadum Mosque itself. It's a rather elaborate complex and seems to have been damaged in more than one phase. The front part of the mosque has been burnt, as was the library next to it. And then again, according to what we found and the statements of eyewitnesses, the top of the minaret, when it was shot off, landed on the library and collapsed the rear wall. Go to the next page. You will see a close-up of the burnt front of the mosque, the charred base of the minaret, and the burnt-out facade of the library, as well as a pre-war photo that shows the extended portico that was burnt down. Then if you go two pages further, you can see the remains of the burnt portico. Again it's clear that this is fire-charred remains. The portico extension was built in the eighteenth century, made largely of wood. And finally, there's an entry for the mosque library which we covered not only as a building but as a cultural institution, and that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. first burnt, and then if you look at the next photo, you can see the collapsed rear wall. We dug around in the rubble and found the remains of the top of the minaret, including most of the fragments of the minaret's carved balcony. So it's very clear that what collapsed the rear here was the toppling of the upper portion of the minaret. So that gives you an idea of the type of documentation we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And the same type of -- the format is all over the database? You can find the same type of information all --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- with all the sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, whether it's mosques, churches, or civil sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And all the sites listed in the indictment, they have been object of assessment --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- by you and Mr. Herscher?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Or by third-party sources such as the IMG database and/the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the exhibit be brought back. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You travelled to Kosovo via The Hague, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you expressed the wish here to work for the purposes of the Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they told you that you wouldn't be working as their agent.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that they are very interested in your activity.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they would like to use your activity as the result of the work of an objective analysis which they have no influence over?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I cannot speak of their intentions, but they gave us no directions as to what our findings should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they give you any instructions at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The kind I outlined, namely what would be -- make useful evidence; photographs. They also told us not to depose witnesses but merely to take basic information and contact information. Basically, they told us to record the facts as we find them, which was also our intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago you said that you looked into all the places that were mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We -- the -- if you look at the indictment, the places which are mentioned and which are represented by photographs here are represented in the amended indictment, which was produced after we had supplied the Tribunal with our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that report of yours coincides with the indictment. You concluded your report in 2001, as you said.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. And we submitted it to the Tribunal in the summer of 2001. The amended indictment, as far as I know, was produced in October of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the indictment was published in May 1999, when the war was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date of the amended indictment? We'll be reminded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 29 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: October '99 [sic]. So what you're saying, Mr. Riedlmayer, is that you produced your report, then there was the amended indictment. It's right that what is in your report is reflected in that amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But not in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the original. The original mentions cultural heritage in generic terms but mentions no specific sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, but I think that this relationship between your work and the indictment has been established. But you said, before giving us that explanation, that when you went to Kosovo via The Hague, that you raised the question of how much your work will be beneficial and useful to the Tribunal and its needs.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We would have gone to Kosovo regardless but we approached the Tribunal because we felt that the kind of work that we were doing might assist them in their work. It does not reflect in any way as to the conclusions of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who paid you for the -- were you paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not paid for the work. Our expenses were paid by the grant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From the foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the foundation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give thought to the findings for the requirements of the Tribunal and the fact as to whether the -- this Tribunal was trying those who committed the bombing and destroyed cultural monuments in Kosovo during the NATO airstrike, the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do. If I understand the question correctly, I must say I pointed out that we took all allegations seriously, including the ones made about NATO damage to cultural heritage sites in Kosovo, and we took great care to investigate them. And if we had found that NATO had damaged these sites, we would have reported accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your oral presentation now, it seems to spring into the first plan or -- like in the newspapers, the front line, what you are asserting, that is to say, that NATO did not damage Serb churches, Serbian churches. Is that your finding and conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That was our finding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your finding that NATO did not damage Serbian churches. How were the Serbian churches damaged then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The damage to Serbian churches that we found can be attributed to attacks after the war by Kosovar Albanians. This is not only our findings, but it is also the official finding of the Serbian Orthodox Diocese of Raska in Prizren. If you look at their documentation in Raspeto [phoen] Kosovo, Krusevat [phoen] Kosovo, it makes it quite clear that these attacks occurred after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave to one side for the time being the fact that I completely challenge the fact that NATO did not damage with its bombs the Serb cultural monuments, but the one you mentioned just now -- what you said just now is something that I would like to ask you. Whose troops throughout that time in Kosovo and Metohija, during the time that you said the Kosovars -- the Albanians destroyed the churches, whose troops were they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Whose troops were what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Whose troops were in Kosovo at the time? The NATO troops, were they in Kosovo and Metohija throughout the time that you consider the churches were destroyed in?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: KFOR was there, which includes, of course, not only NATO but Russian and other forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you just mentioned this publication by the Serbian Church, which I see Mr. Wladimiroff holding in his hands just now. And they have flags, the flags of countries showing whose troops are responsible for the security of the territory in which those churches were destroyed. I didn't see any Russian ones, but I did see American, Italian, French, German flags, et cetera. Now, are those states responsible for the destruction of the cultural monuments in areas protected by their troops?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to say. He's here giving evidence about the damage, not about the responsibility or otherwise of KFOR, which is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's a different issue, I don't think I can agree that that is not relevant, because Mr. Riedlmayer in his report speaks about the causes and ways in which the cultural monuments were destroyed and damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him if he found out while he was in Kosovo who was responsible for the security of the various churches and if he knows anything about how they came to be destroyed, despite that responsibility. Now, can you help us to that, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to a degree. Our primary task was to assess the condition of the buildings rather than the security atmosphere. We did find that most Serbian Orthodox churches that we came across, such as the Pec Patriarchate or the churches in Prizren, and numerous churches in various areas such as in south-eastern Kosovo, in the Pomoravia [phoen], all had heavy NATO guard in front of them. On the other hand, a number of ruined churches in abandoned villages had no guards on them, and we brought up this issue in our conversation with UNMIK officials in Pristina and urged them to provide protection for all churches, whether they are intact or not and whether they are world-class sites or village sites. But that was the extent of our involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, in preparing your work, had in mind the requirements of the Tribunal's indictment, on the one hand; and on the other, did you have any instructions? Did you receive any instructions by the financiers of your project? And you said that they were the -- it was the Centre for Middle Eastern Studies at Harvard, I believe, and the Packard Centre. And so was it Packard, Harvard, and the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We received instructions from none of these as to what we should look at. We did not perform the study in order to support any particular indictment. We hoped that the results of our investigations would help bring to justice whoever targeted cultural and religious heritage in Kosovo. As far as our sponsors and funders are concerned, they supported us, but they gave us no instructions whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you expect, in view of the fact that your report was financed and carried out, do you expect the subjects, that is to say, the countries -- or rather, the country that led the NATO aggression, including you too, can be accepted as being objective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness. You can ask him if -- you can ask him this: What's suggested is that your evidence is not objective, Mr. Riedlmayer. It was, I guess, what's been alleged. Now, can you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Just deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an American national. However, if we had found evidence that NATO had destroyed heritage, we would have reported it all the same. We were not working for the government. Our conclusions are entirely our own and our own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you use, in the course of your investigations and research, facts and figures and information by NATO but also by the Yugoslav authorities, Yugoslav state institutions, as to the dates and locations of the NATO airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely. We took all available information into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did have in mind the NATO information and the locations by NATO and the Yugoslav organs as to the dates and locations of the NATO airstrikes; is that correct? You had these?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We had the locations that were cited. The allegations primarily came from the Yugoslav sources, and so those had a heavier weight in our choice of sites. What NATO statements and photographs were published were largely in reaction to Yugoslav allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know the percentage and share, as you conducted research and investigation, what the share and percentage was of Christian and how much of the Ottoman cultural heritage? What was the ratio in Kosovo and Metohija? Let me make myself clearer. I'm not talking about the absolute number of all churches and so on, but what comes under the term of "cultural heritage," Christian and Ottoman, in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. As our report makes clear, it is very hard to come up with statistics. Serbian sources generally speak of a thousand or more Orthodox sites, but in fact many of these are archeological sites rather than standing buildings. And by the parameters of our survey, we concluded archeological sites. They're not as vulnerable to damage and they tend to be harder to document in terms of pre-war photographs. So we did not visit archeological sites, whether Stone Age or medieval. In terms of actual standing monuments, we went by a publication of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of the Republic of Serbia, published in the spring of 1999, which lists approximately 210 Orthodox sites that were under protection. However, out of those, approximately 40 were twentieth-century buildings. So it's -- that's a rough number. In terms of the Ottoman heritage, it's also very complicated. The construction during the Ottoman period included some Christian monuments. For example, the Pec Patriarchate was enlarged several times under Ottoman rule. Out of the -- I assume you mean mosques, and if you mean mosques, out of the 600-odd mosques, roughly half or more were of the Ottoman period. There was very little construction after the fall of the Ottoman rule in Kosovo, of mosques, until the 1980s, when there was an increase of construction of houses of worship, both Christian and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you observe and take note of the fact that in that respect, until the war began and the destruction began, there was no discrimination with respect to the construction both of Christian and Muslim religious buildings in Kosovo? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That wasn't part of our survey. We did observe the fact that as opposed to 210, approximately, Orthodox sites in Kosovo, only about 15 to 20 mosques were under official legal protection. So what discrimination there was was certainly in terms of the attention paid to these monuments by the official organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the form of attention or in the form of the actual state of affairs with respect to the buildings that make up the cultural heritage and their state?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: What I mean is in terms of the amount of state monies for restoration and conservation, of which the majority went to officially listed sites, and since more of the officially listed sites were Orthodox, more of the money was spent on the Orthodox sites. Also in terms of the actual protection, in legal terms, a number of the listed monuments that were mosques had been badly altered by unauthorised repairs, it seemed, in recent decades, without apparently being stopped by the authorities, even though these were listed monuments. But that wasn't the principal focus of our study.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know that in professional assessments, which I assume are objective because they do not only refer to Yugoslav institutions, that the share of Christian in relation to Ottoman cultural heritage in Kosovo and Metohija is somewhere between 75:25 -- the ratio is 75:25, that that is roughly the ratio? Are you aware of that ratio?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And apart from this latest publication, from which you quoted a moment ago and said that you used the 1999 institute for the Serbian cultural heritage, did you use any other Serbian publications, historical documents, books related to the history of art, and so on and so forth, which relate to the buildings that you investigated, the sites you investigated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you will look at a number of these entries, which have extensive bibliographies, you will see that we covered all the available literature. We looked at Yugoslav art historical journals, the annuals of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Kosovo, of Serbia, international publications. There's a recent monograph by Gojko Subotic which covers Serbian heritage in Kosovo encyclopedically. We invested a lot of preparation before ever going to Kosovo, and we continued to track publications that appeared after our initial field work, to the extent that we were able.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And of these consultations and the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments in Pristina and Prizren, did you include those too?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that it would be logical if an international expert team would have been set up to look into the state of affairs and to investigate and research the state of cultural and historical monuments in Kosovo which would be able to avoid a partial approach, or an approach under the shadows of this Tribunal, or the financing of it from countries which led the aggression against Yugoslavia? Did you ever give thought to that? Would that be of value? Would that have been beneficial, in view of the fact that one of the most interesting places on the continent of Europe was worthy of the attentions of an objective international expert team of professionals instead of the kind of approach that we have here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that seems to be making the same point again, that this witness's work is not objective, and he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I have a specific, concrete question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the letter from Slobodan Curcic, a respected art historian and professor, to your colleagues from Princeton, for example, which was published in the USA ECOMOS May/June 2000, and it assessed your report as one-sided because they said that it referred for the most part to Islamic cultural monuments?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm aware of it, yes. What Mr. Milosevic seems to be referring to was the publication of a preliminary version of our report in the newsletter of the US committee for ECOMOS, the International Council on Monuments and Sites. In the subsequent issue, Professor Curcic wrote a letter to the editor in which he misconstrued our report quite dramatically, claimed that we had not covered any Serbian Orthodox sites, and made some allegations about our findings. I'm aware of it. I think it's completely mistaken on Professor Curcic's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. You differ there, and that is allowed. A difference of opinion is allowed. Have you heard of a pamphlet, a pamphlet this time, by the Islamic religious community in Kosovo, under the title of, "Serbian Barbarism Against Islamic Monuments in Kosovo," February 1988, published in Pristina in the year 2000? Did you happen to have this pamphlet in your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I've seen the book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the photographs, some of the photographs, or perhaps some of the findings from that pamphlet, which was compiled by Sabri Bajgora, whom you mentioned otherwise, did you take them over from that pamphlet of his?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We did not. We examined the photographs that the Islamic community had collected in October of 1999 and took originals of the photographs at that time. Subsequently, when the Islamic community published this actually small book, they used some of the same photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who Sabri Bajgora is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. He is the assistant mufti, second in the hierarchy of the Islamic religious community in Kosovo, and he's professor at the Faculty of Islamic Studies in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he specialises in Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Sabri Bajgora, whom you consider to be a relevant source, is he scientifically qualified to assess the condition of cultural heritage in Kosovo? Do you consider him to be a qualified expert to assess the state of cultural heritage in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No. He's not a conservation professional, and we did not ask for his opinion on things. We simply asked him for photographs, concerning which we made our own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is now in fact 3.00. It's time to adjourn for a short period. We'll adjourn for quarter of an hour. Mr. Riedlmayer, will you remember in this and any other adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence, including members of the Prosecution team, until it's over. Yes. 3.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the period between 1960 and 1981, the Albanian separatists plundered and destroyed the monasteries of Dejavici [phoen], Decani. And on the 16th of May, 1981, they attacked the Pec Patriarchate and set fire to it, and the monastery konak was burnt down, containing vast artistic works of great value. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That period was not part of our study, but yes, I've heard reports of that. I've also read that police at the time claimed that it -- the fire at the konak was accidental. But as I say, I am not in a position to speak about any of that from first hand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, since I assume your report covers that period, that the terrorist KLA, on the 22nd of July, 1998, broke into the monastery of St. Kosme and Damjan near Orahovac and that they seriously damaged the walls of the monastery konak? Did you omit to mention that, or do you have any information about it as part of your research project?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I assume what you're referring to is the monastery at Zociste south of Orahovac. Yes, it is included in our database. Not only was the konak damaged, but subsequently the church next to the monastery was destroyed with explosives. My understanding is that it is now being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the NATO airstrike on the 22nd of March, 1999 - that was the fifth day of the war - a rocket hit and destroyed the museum building of the Prizren League, which can be shown on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be please shown to the witness. We can see that it was hit from above. This is the building of the Prizren League, so please show the witness both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you see it, it could not have been destroyed from the ground, as you are claiming.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a site that we went to document, and we have numerous photographs from before and, of course, the condition in 1989 when it was nothing but a levelled site. However, I would like to point out a number of things in this particular case. What caused us to conclude that this was destroyed from the ground up was, first of all, if you look on either side here, the former Prizren League Museum was an early nineteenth century small, two-storey building surrounded on two sides by other historic buildings. The buildings here to the left and behind it are also part of the museum, and then the other buildings on this side. What is particularly striking even about this photograph is that these buildings which are at a distance of, at most, five to ten metres from the site are completely undamaged, which speaks against any high explosive. Secondly, the construction of the Prizren League Museum is what is known in the region as carpic [phoen]. It's a mud-brick building. It's wooden beams, and the interstices are filled with unfired brick. Typically, that kind of building cannot withstand either fire or explosives very well. It just falls apart. If this building had been hit by something with a heavy explosive charge, you wouldn't see this much of it remaining. What I can see here is very typical of a number of other buildings we saw elsewhere in Kosovo which were clearly burned down, often in an even tighter urban context, with undamaged buildings less than two metres away. So I would rather doubt that this was hit. It's also a matter of logic. Why this building, the one monument in Prizren that is a monument to the Albanian national movement, would be the one monument in Prizren that was supposedly hit by a NATO airstrike as an intentional kind of act. It makes very little sense. Could you show the other side, please. You can see here charred beams sticking up from the top and the ground storey still standing. I have numerous pre-destruction photos of the building. You can see there wasn't really that much more to it. Finally, of course there were also a number of people we interviewed who claimed to have seen the destruction which they say was done by Serbian police firing hand-held incendiary devices. Finally, between the Prizren League Museum and the buildings immediately to the back of it were a series of life-sized statues of the founders of the League of Prizren. Those statues were subsequently, after the war, fished out of the river. Again that speaks to the probability that the destruction was malicious and from the ground up rather than that the statues were lifted up and taken into the river by some airstrike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the other photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No the other side, please. As you can see, it was hit from above, and it could not have been hit by any hand-held rocket launcher. And on the 28th of March, 1999, it was hit directly by a rocket from a plane. Is convincing proof what Albanian witnesses will tell you? Is your logic convincing? Why would NATO hit a cultural monument of the Albanians, if I ask you why did NATO strike a column of Albanian refugees where dozens of men, women, and children were killed? Why would NATO strike again a second column of Albanian refugees where again dozens of Albanians, men, women, and children, were killed? Why would NATO strike a bus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- on the line from Kosovo to Pec?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a question? The witness says -- the witness says -- just a moment. Just a moment. What the witness says are from his conclusions this building was set fire to. Now, if you want to put something different to him, do, but you've heard what his conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see on this photograph - please put it on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- there are no traces of fire there. It's clearly a photograph of a house hit from the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The upper storey, which no longer exists on this, has three tall windows and a wood-timbered tile roof. What you see here is collapsed roof timbers. What is sticking up looks charred, and there's something that looks like smoke rising up from the building. That's all I can tell from the picture. When we went to Prizren, the site had been completely levelled, and they were about to construct a replica of it. What I can tell is that the buildings next to it, upon our visit, were still in the same condition as you can see on this picture, with the tile roofs and the old windows still intact, the paint flaking. Obviously they had not been re-glazed. Any kind of explosion would at the very least have shattered the windows, and you would have been able to see that these are repaired windows. The distance is very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, NATO hit my house with three rockets. Twelve metres from the house, not a single pane of a glass was broken, a building twelve metres away from the same garden. Are you a ballistics expert?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do not claim to be. I'm simply stating what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on, then. Do you know that the area around the Pec Patriarchate, that was built in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, was hit by NATO planes on a number of occasions - on the 31st of March, the 1st of April, the 11th, the 12th and the 17th of May, 1999 - even though it is a monument in the first category, which UNESCO placed on the World Heritage list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's put to you that it was hit three times, the Patriarchate. Would you deal with that, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We visited the Patriarchate, as did two independent conservation experts who checked the buildings and murals and found no sign of damage other than that from rising damp and long-term deferred maintenance. The two conservation experts were Tody Cezar, who is mentioned in our report, who was an independent consultant for UNMIK's Department of Culture in December of 2000 and January 2001. More recently, a team from the Italian Instituto Centrale Del Estero visited both the Patriarchate at Pec and the monastery in Decani, and in a published account in Giornali Del Arte, published last fall, they state that there was no war damage to be seen at either site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot interrupt you. I didn't say that it was hit. I said that they bombed the area of the Pec Patriarchate on the 1st of March, the 1st of April, the 11th and 12th and 17th of May, 1999. And you said that the information about bombing was provided to you both by NATO and the Yugoslav authorities. So my question was: Did you know that the area of the Pec Patriarchate was targeted five times in 1999, regardless of your own findings? Let me go on to my next question anyway. The area of the Gracanica monastery --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. It's suggested that the area was targeted, not the Patriarchate itself, but the area. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All I can say is: Yes, I read the allegation, which is why we looked at whether there was any damage to the building, and the suggestion is that there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And the area around the Gracanica monastery. You know that that is one of the most beautiful buildings of world architecture. It dates back to the fourteenth century and it is protected as a world-class monument. That the area of the Gracanica monastery was bombed by NATO on the 28th, the 3rd of March, the 10th of April, the 1st, 14th, and 17th of May. The rockets fell close to the monastery. They didn't hit the monastery itself, but they did cause damage to the facade of the monastery and the fresco paintings. Did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again, I have no first-hand knowledge of the events during the war. Obviously I wasn't there. As far as the monastery goes, again we have the report of Ms. Tody Cezar, who visited the monastery and found that the frescos were endangered by rising damp caused by groundwater and by the failure of pointing, that is, mortar coming out from between the bricks, which is a result of lack of maintenance over the years. As far as any damage, we didn't see any, and the monks didn't tell us of any at the time. I'm aware that there are allegations that such damage existed. We didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not on the spot, and I understand that, but are you familiar with the report by experts of the Republican Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments of Serbia on the state of the fresco paintings in Gracanica, published by the Society of Conservators in Belgrade, 2000, by editor Marko Omcikus? Are you familiar with that report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the citation to the work. I was not able to get a hold of a copy of that particular journal. However, the report was summarised in an article by Professor Slobodan Curcic in the journal British Byzantine Studies. In this, he repeats the assertion by the conservators that the frescos had separated from the wall and were in danger of collapse. This does not match with the assessment that we have from the conservator Ms. Cezar. I don't claim to be an expert on mural paintings myself, so all I can state is that we have two reports by experts which seem to be at variance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're mentioning the professor from Princeton?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that NATO planes directly targeted the memorial complex Gazimestan? Let me remind you. It is a memorial complex of the Kosovo battle from 1389 on the 13th of April, the 22nd, 23rd of May, and the 1st of June, and that they damaged the Gazimestan memorial complex.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Gazimestan complex, which is north of Pristina, in the municipality of Obilic, was one of the sites we visited precisely because of these allegations, which we were eager to check out. We looked very carefully all around the monument and we observed only one kind of damage. Surrounding the Gazimestan memorial are a number of concrete tubes which hold spotlights. These concrete tubes had cast-iron ornamentation put on it; a Serbian cross with the dates 1389 and 1989, commemorating the 600th anniversary. Somebody had apparently come and ripped off the cast-iron ornamentation. You could still see the dirt shadow where the cast-iron had been affixed to the concrete. The memorial itself looked completely undamaged, but we were told by a UN policeman on the site that the interior staircase had been damaged by an explosive placed inside after the war; however, there was no trace of it from the outside. We were not allowed access to the inside. In short, what damage we saw was not consistent with anything that could have been caused by an aerial attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 3rd of April, 1999, in the NATO airstrikes, St. Nicholas church was damaged in Djurakovac, built in the fourteenth century?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Djurakovac is another one of the sites that Ms. Tody Cezar visited. It looks in perfectly good condition. It has some nuns still staying in there, and they mentioned no damage. It is under the guard of Portuguese troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The St. Nicholas church was damaged in Djurakovac, near Istok, fourteenth-century church. Do you know that on the night between the 14th and 15th of April, when attacking Klina, in the village of Drsnik, that NATO damaged the Paraskeva church and destroyed the belfry of the church? Of course, after Italian units of KFOR arrived, the Albanian terrorists, in June 1999, demolished the church and seriously damaged, by explosives, the same church, and they razed the village to the ground. Are you aware of this damage caused by NATO airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Drsnik was the example that I showed photos of. The belfry was intact. It was a modern belfry of some age, with a metal structure. The building itself had walls and roof completely intact. The interior had had a fire set in it and the walls had been defaced, as I showed. Again, this is not something that I would believe could have been caused by airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the same site, the church of St. Paraskeva?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right. It's the two pictures I showed at the conclusion of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that NATO air forces, on the 2nd, 4th, and 10th of May, 1999, targeted and damaged St. Gavrilo at Draganac, one of the most valuable monuments in Kosovo, near Gnjilane, and it is a protected site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm not aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please show this map. It's a map of Kosovo, showing the churches, monasteries, and cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have in mind this distribution, and did you see anywhere in the world more densely scattered monasteries, churches, and monuments of cultural heritage as you see on this small area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I am familiar with the map. What the map does not show, which is seen in other versions of this map, such as in Gojko Subotic's book, is the fact that many of these sites are in fact archeological sites rather than standing churches. Nevertheless, I do agree that Kosovo is indeed a treasure house of architecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 14th and 24th of May, NATO targeted and damaged the church of St. Archangel in Nerodimlje near Urosevac - it dates back to the fourteenth century - and Albanian terrorists, after the arrival of American KFOR troops, demolished, burnt, and blew up this church, as they did St. Nicholas, St. Stefan, and the Ascension of Mother Mary?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. We have recorded all of these sites in our survey. If you look at the map of destroyed Serbian Orthodox heritage in our survey, you will find a cluster near Urosevac. It's hard to see on this black-and-white copy, but you can see -- you can see right here a cluster of dots, rather large ones, because they represent multiple buildings near Urosevac. Those are the churches at Nerodimlje. However, based on information we received from the Serbian Orthodox eparchy of Raske and Prizren, we recorded these churches as having been destroyed after the war, during the summer of 1999, by Albanians. Obviously, a place that had been blown up leaves no evidence of what may have happened to it before, but as far as I know, the Serbian Orthodox eparchy does not allege that they were destroyed during the war but after the war. But our database has pictures and assessments of each of these monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Albanians perhaps raze it to the ground in order to destroy traces of NATO airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I cannot speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There are documents about that. Are you aware that on the 1st, 14th, and 16th of April, when the area of Kutlovac [phoen] was targeted, the old square, that NATO damaged the Zvecan medieval fortress, a medieval fortress near Kosovska Mitrovica from the twelfth century, a world-class monument? The walls of the fortress were seriously damaged during those airstrikes. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I paid a brief visit to Zvecan when I was in Mitrovica last March. It is a ruined fortress, and I didn't see any evidence of recent damage, but of course it's very hard to tell with an archeological ruin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware how many of these numerous mosques in Kosmat were built in the last ten-year period? But not ten years. Let's take the period from 1993 to 1999, that seven-year period prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did not do a statistical analysis in our database, but I could very easily. I'm aware that a large number of churches and mosques were built in Kosovo in the 1980s and 1990s, in part because with the easing of church/state relations after the decline of Communism, it became legally possible, and in part because it became financially possible. In the case of mosques, a number of Kosovars who worked in Western Europe sent home money. In the case of churches, there were a number of well-to-do Kosovar Serbs who expended their money by building churches, such as the Karic brothers. These new mosques and churches were often targeted when -- and then they were destroyed, and -- but so were some of the older ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the period from 1987 until 1999, several hundred mosques were built in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have never seen that statistic. The number seems large to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume that you do make a distinction between monuments of culture and ordinary religious monuments built, shall we say, in this last period from 1987 until 1999? I assume that you do make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we do make the distinction.
