However, because of the fact that a number of very recently built Orthodox sites were on the list of protected monuments, such as, for example, the memorial church in Djakovica which was completed right on the eve of the war in 1998/1999, and because of the fact that religious monuments in general seem to be singled out for destruction, we decided not to limit our survey to officially listed monuments but to include all religious structures. The distinction is always marked in our database where there's a separate line about whether or not a building has listed status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there must be a different attitude among ordinary citizens and believers towards what is a historical monument and is part of the cultural heritage and a newly built religious building. So in the feelings of people, in the motives regarding protection and use, that the people too make a distinction in that respect.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Maybe so. Nevertheless, if you look at the list of damaged or destroyed Orthodox churches that were targeted after the war, many of them date from recent times. So whether it's a mosque or a church, it means something to people whether it's been around for hundreds of years or whether it's recently built. It fulfils its cultural and religious function. So we believed that we ought to cover these as well, but obviously our initial starting point was the listed monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about monuments that are protected. How many mosques in Kosovo were listed as monuments of culture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It depends on who does the listing and at which period. It seemed that there were several revisions of the official list for protection from the 1980s onwards. So it's hard to pin down an exact figure. But between 15 and 30, according to various documents and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 30 on the outside. That would be the maximum.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you see how you reach the ratio that I referred to earlier on. You said that in 1998 and 1999, 225 mosques were destroyed or damaged, and it follows from what you have just said that these were -- that this was not a significant percentage of them that were listed as protected cultural monuments.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That does not follow at all. First of all, if you do an analysis, the number of listed monuments that were hit was quite high. And in addition to that, we note in our report that a number of culturally and architecturally and historically significant mosques were not included in the official listing. We assume on the basis value judgements and political motives, because otherwise you could not explain the discrepancy. For example, we noticed that in the region of Pec, the number of mosques -- if you bear with me for a moment. I have here -- there were 36 mosques. Half of those mosques - so we're talking 18 of them - dated from the fifteenth through the eighteenth centuries, and yet of those 18 mosques, I believe no more than two or three were on the officially protected list. So I think it's clear that the listed status of a monument does not necessarily in this context indicate that it is historically or architecturally significant. It simply reflects administrative and political priorities which in my judgement have affected decisions on whether to list or not to list the monument for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your assessment that it was not professional criteria but political criteria that we used when the experts of Serbia and Yugoslavia and Kosovo and so on categorised monuments of culture?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm not impugning the professional qualifications of these experts, but I do believe that political considerations played some part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that numerous monuments of culture from the Ottoman period, the Ottoman heritage - I'm not talking about the Christian ones now - were renewed, repaired, and protected by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Serbia, that is, by the Government of Serbia, such as, for instance, the Sinan Pasha Mosque and the hamam in Prizren, and that a series of such significant monuments were maintained, conserved? Do you know, for instance, that in the 1990s, the government reconstructed the Imperial and Jasar Pasha mosque in Pristina and the Bajrakli mosque in Pec, and the Terzija bridge in Djakovica, and that all these are first-class listed monuments? Are you aware of all these significant monuments that I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I am aware of these monuments. I'm also aware that in the case of some of them, there was conservation work done on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that the turbe of Sultan Murat, where he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. died at the Battle of Kosovo, was never damaged by the Serbs? I assume that you saw that turbe or mausoleum?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I visited it, and it was intact, although very badly in need of restoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, that Sinan Pasha, the Sinan Pasha mosque in Prizren, which was built in the seventeenth century, was built by the material that had been used previously to build the Christian monastery of the Archangel which was destroyed in order to have the mosque built, and that that mosque once again, the one dating back to the seventeenth century, regardless of that, was listed in the first category, "Word Class Site," and maintained by the government and its institutions? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a large number of mosques during the war was used by the KLA, especially their minarets, as sniper nests and that they were legitimate military targets in that case? Are you aware of that? Because you delved into the reasons for the destruction of the cultural monuments, I assume.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing what happened during the war. What I can tell you is that in many cases where we saw mosques burnt out, minarets decapitated, we did not see any signs that the mosques had been targeted by small-arms fire, which I would assume is the -- would have been the result of a firefight with KLA or snipers. But I'm not a military expert, so I couldn't begin to tell you. What I can tell you is that in many cases, not only were the mosques damaged or destroyed, but there was extensive evidence of defacement, things like scriptures torn from their covers and scattered on the ground, sometimes defaced with human excrement. The walls full of Serbian graffiti, obscenities, anti-Albanian or anti-NATO slogans. Clearly those are not attributable to legitimate military action. That's all I can say on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As to the graffiti, the whole world knows about graffiti, and they are a characteristic feature everywhere. But do you know, for example, that the Hadum Mosque in Djakovica, which was not directly targeted by NATO, but when it targeted places in Djakovica, it did significantly destroy it on the 10th, 14th and 15th of April when the mosque was in fact destroyed in the bombing although it was not a direct target? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Hadum Mosque in Djakovica is one of the sites that we have documented very extensively. It is in the booklet you see there. We found, first of all, no sign that it had been subjected to explosive damage. The front end had been burnt down. There had been an attempt to burn the interior. The minaret was decapitated, and you could see on the minaret several small round holes. Again, I'm not a military expert, but I would suggest that somebody was using something other than a missile to -- than an aerial missile to decapitate the minaret. Similarly, the library was burnt out. The airstrike damage in Djakovica is -- is quite visible. There's a big Yugoslav army base on the outskirts of town which was very thoroughly flattened, but surrounding houses seemed in reasonable condition. And this site was at some considerable distance from the centre of the old town, which looked like it had been damaged by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the members of the KLA, on the 4th of May, attacked from the surrounding hills of Djakovica, and right up to the 14th of May there was fighting in the area around Hadum Mosque and the marketplace, and that in a repeated attack by NATO on the 25th of May, a direct hit destroyed the large marketplace or, rather, the old centre of town? I think in your report you have made mention of the fact that somebody else did that and not NATO in that airstrike.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, again with a caveat that I'm not a military expert, I can tell you that we did a very extensive survey of the damage to the marketplace, and the damage seemed to be very circumscribed. It was limited to rows of shops directly facing the main street. The rows of buildings behind them tended to be in good shape. The shops all looked burnt down; the interiors completely charred, the timbers of the front and the roof gone. However, the partition walls behind them were, in most cases, perfectly intact. And I would suggest that both the pattern of destruction and the nature of destruction would indicate that this was arson rather than things done from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we quite obviously don't agree on that. We began with the Prizren rebuilding, and you yourself said that you were not a ballistics expert, do you really not consider that it would be a good idea for some experts to take a look at it and to ascertain whether what I am claiming is the truth or whether your findings are the right ones, of a non-ballistic expert and so on, especially if we bear in mind the information about fighting in Djakovica which went on for a full ten days and the bombing of the old marketplace and that in that fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not a matter for the witness. He's given his evidence as to what he's seen. He's given his conclusions. You're saying there should be another expert. Well, that's a matter for others. It's not for the witness to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not saying that another expert witness should be brought in, Mr. May, and I'm not suggesting anything to the witness. All I'm doing is asking him for his opinion in view of the fact that he is making assessments and evaluations about things that he himself said he did not understand. Does he consider that a group of experts, who are well-versed in what neither I myself nor the witness is well-versed in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have made the point. I have made the point, and it is a ruling, that this is not a matter for this witness. You asked him about the damage. He gave the best answer he could. Now, if you have any further comments, you can make them, the Prosecution can make them, but we're not getting anywhere by this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me continue with my questions then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Petrik -- is Petrik Domi [phoen]? I think you mentioned him and said he secretly filmed the burning of the marketplace in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Petrik Domi was a young resident of Djakovica. His photos were distributed by wire service agencies after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the war therefore. And do you know that, during the war, he was a member of the 124th Brigade of the terrorist KLA?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that that material of his was in fact rigged, just as on many occasions was the case of the wars on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have no information of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that the mosque in Landovica, which you visited, is only 20 metres away from the Prizren-Djakovica road, where at the end of January 1995, from the minaret of that mosque, a column of the Yugoslav army was targeted? And at that time in Kosovo, the Verification Mission was in place.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I only described the damage. I have no information about what may have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any information and were you interested at all in taking a look at how many mosques were destroyed in the area where the fighting went on with the so-called KLA and how many in the area where there was no fighting? I'm asking you this in view of the fact that you put forward your facts for the indictment and some which should be relevant for an assessment of that information and those facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: If you look on page 14 of the report, it has the distribution on a map. If you could turn on the ELMO. If you could try to focus it so it's all there. Okay. That's good enough. A little bit more. Good. As you can see, the pattern of -- this is the map of damage to Islamic religious sites. You can see that the pattern of destruction covers much of Kosovo. There are significant exceptions. The city of Prizren has no damage sites, whereas Djakovica, Pec, Mitrovica have large numbers of damage sites. In Pristina, only one mosque was burnt, as well as the archives of the Islamic community. Similarly, there were relatively low numbers in other towns. However, villages all the way from the north to the south were targeted. Significant exceptions include the southernmost tip, the Gora region, which is Muslim but not Albanian. The Goranci are Slavs who are Muslim. There was a very heavy destruction in the area roughly between Prizren, Djakovica, and Suva Reka, where a significant exception was the village of Mamusa, which is mainly ethnically Turkish. There, the mosque was intact. But most other villages in the surrounding region, the mosques were destroyed or damaged. Otherwise, there was less damage to be seen in Eastern Kosovo where there is a fairly heavy Serbian population; in Kamenica region, Novo Brdo, around Strpce, which is mainly an ethnic Serb region, as well as the far north, but otherwise, you see a fairly general pattern going on. Some of it is also a question of the distribution of mosques. There were relatively few mosques in the Drenica region. What few there were were mostly damaged or destroyed. That's all I can say about patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less what you have just said coincides with the assumption that where there was combat between the army and the police on one side and the terrorist KLA on the other, there was much greater damage, immeasurably greater than where the Serb population was in the majority and where, if we assume that the Serbs destroyed mosques, you would expect the mosques to be destroyed more than in where the fighting was going on. Now, do you know what period, because I'm sure you deal with this, when the most -- when the oldest monument to Albanian architecture dates back to? And can you tell us what that monument is? What is the oldest monument?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think that's a question of definitions. Whether you call a mosque an Albanian monument or an Islamic monument is a question. Whether you call a medieval residential site one or the other is a question of definitions of ethnicity. The oldest Islamic sites date back to the early fourteenth century. Residential architecture tends to be on the whole more recent, as you would expect that people rebuild their houses quite often. But I'm not sure what the point of the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point of the question is that you have been speaking and not differentiating between monuments of the Ottoman-Turkish architectural type, and I'm asking you to tell me the oldest monument to Albanian architecture. So we're not talking about the Ottoman and Turkish architecture here but Albanian architecture. What is the oldest monument to Albanian architecture in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't necessarily want to get into long historical arguments, respecting the Court, but I would posit that the people who built the mosques in Kosovo over the nearly 600 years that there has been Islam in Kosovo had been, in the main part and especially in the villages, Albanians, also in the towns. For example, in Pec, one of the mosques that was -- we found destroyed was the Kursumli xhamia. You would call it an Ottoman monument, but the founder of the mosque was an Albanian native of Pec, Husein Pasa, who became Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire. The Ottoman Empire was not a nation state, and everyone who was in the empire participated, to one degree or another, in the common cultural enterprise. So it's very hard to sort out, in the culture of those 600 years, what belongs to which nationality. I think the question, to a degree, is somewhat absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is absurd, because, for example, the Grand Vizier of the Turkish sultan, Sulejman II The Magnificent, was Mehmed Pasa Sokolovic, who was a Serb by origin. But we do not consider that what he built, the buildings he built all over Turkey, is the subject of Serb architecture. And the same holds true vice versa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the significance for these proceedings of all this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With these proceedings, nothing at all. It has to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on to another topic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But are you aware of the fact that NATO, on several attempts, on the 10th, the 14th, and 15th of April, in the course of May 1992 [as interpreted], directly targeted the old marketplace of Pec, which was destroyed, which is where the Bajrakli mosque is, the first-class, world-listed monument which was devastated in part?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm aware of the allegations. We also investigated it, as we did all of these allegations. With respect to the Bajrakli xhamia, we have extensive documentation. I can tell you, first of all, the roof and the walls of the mosque are completely intact, the interior completely burnt out. Even the door was intact but charred. I fail to see how this could be attributed to bombing, again with the caveat that I'm not a military expert. I can, however, tell you that the interior of the mosque, up to about a five-metre height, was exposed to very high temperatures, suggesting the use of some sort of accelerant to create the fire. The furnishings of mosques are very sparse. There are only carpets. And in the absence of some kind of flammable, it's very hard to set fire to one that does not have wooden elements, as this one does not. The heat was so high that marble columns holding up the women's balcony were completely cracked by the fire, that the surface of the pulpit, which was hand-carved of marble and dated from the fifteenth century, had in part been turned to powdery burnt lime. I would suggest that the mosque was not collateral damage from bombing but a victim of arson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean collateral damage during the bombing of the marketplace in Pec?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is what was suggested, and I suggest that was not the case. In the case of the marketplace, the pattern of damage was very similar to that of Djakovica. The shops on either side of the main market street were badly charred, houses just one row behind were perfectly intact, and this for several blocks in length. I can describe the damage. I leave the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claimed that the Catholic church of St. Anthony in Djakovica was not damaged by the bombing, although there is a fact, and I want to ask you about it, and that is: Do you know that on the 29th of March, 1999, during the attack on Djakovica, it was precisely NATO planes that damaged the St. Anthony Church, and the whole front wall above the entrance to the church was split and the nuns' part -- that the wall cracked? And as far as I remember, this was justified as being collateral damage. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We visited the church and talked to the parish priest, who was present in Djakovica throughout the war, and we have his account of what happened. And according to his account, the Yugoslav army troops ejected him and the nuns from the friary and took over the church and the parish buildings as their operational quarters half an hour before the NATO airstrikes. The church looked perfectly fine. It had had no repair work done on it since the war, and we were there in October 1999. The parish buildings had new windows, and they were busy repainting them because the interior had been badly vandalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that when the army went to the konak of that church was a crime, to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It is not for me to make legal determinations. However, I understand that the use of buildings that are protected under international law is analogous to the abuse of the Red Cross symbols, and therefore it's not legitimate. But as I say, I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Although you're not a lawyer, you consider that it was a violation of the law, or abuse equal to the abuse of the Red Cross symbols. Now, as you consider that, could you tell me how you characterised the aggression of the NATO pact on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not for the witness to deal with. Now, Mr. Milosevic, we're coming to the time when we're going to adjourn. You've been cross-examining this witness for very nearly an hour and 40 minutes. We shall expect you to wind up tomorrow morning fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't been able to complete my questions because I didn't expect this witness, Mr. May. As you well know, this witness turned up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning we'll go on. Mr. Nice, what is the position after this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no witness, apart from this witness, for tomorrow, because of events concerning a witness who might have been called today. We then have a slightly tricky position on Thursday and Friday. A witness, General Drewienkiewicz, is due to give evidence, and although, as I think I told you earlier today, he's going to produce a considerable quantity of material, it had been hoped to fit him into Thursday and Friday if we had full sitting days. Of course, Thursday and Friday are now not going to be absolutely full days, and I'm concerned that it may not be possible to have his evidence completed in two days. I'm not sure how difficult it's going to be for him to stay over or to be available for next Monday. I'm hoping it may be possible, but it's certainly going to be extremely difficult. I mention that because, of course, the Chamber had had it in mind to deal with some administrative matters and some general topics at the end of the week, by which we took Your Honour to mean Thursday or Friday. When this witness is concluded, might tomorrow be suitable? Although it will be difficult for us, I think, to have got all the answers to Your Honours' questions by then, I've already started the process of speeding up our work on those questions to see if they could be dealt with tomorrow if everybody else would be in a position to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It will obviously be convenient, then, to deal with those matters tomorrow, the procedural matters. We'll have time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As for the witness that you mentioned, you say Thursday is not a full day. My recollection is that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My mistake. Thursday is, Friday isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Entirely my -- can I mention something else, just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply because I'm on my feet, rather than having us popping up and down, I'm mentioning something on Ms. Romano's behalf relating to this witness's evidence. There is a question that arises about the two exhibits shown to him -- two documents shown to him by the accused, which he was able to deal with, and whether they should become exhibits. And secondly, I understand that there is a CD, or CD-ROM, whatever these things are called, detailing all of the survey, containing all the photographs of the survey, which it hadn't been possible for the unit here to reproduce in time for today but which it probably will be possible for them to have got produced for tomorrow. Now, in light of the very extensive questions that have been asked of the witness by the accused, the witness might prefer to be in a position, as he would be tomorrow, to deal with some of those issues by the CD-ROM, which can be produced for the Chamber, and indeed for the accused, to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Apparently the amici and the accused have the material already, but I think Your Honours may be assisted by having this as well tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do not want to retain the witness too long tomorrow, if that can be avoided. We'll consider that in the morning. As for the other two photographs, I don't know where they have got to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think one of them -- I think they've gone back to the accused. Obviously I haven't discussed the issue with Mr. Riedlmayer, but it may be that he will have a view on whether he could explain some of these very detailed answers he's giving about particular buildings of which the accused asked him by reference to the CD-ROM. I don't know what his answer will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's heard that. He can consider it overnight. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, half past 9.00. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of April 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
